     CLOSING BRIEF OF NARUNA INVESTMENTS, LLC, SCOTT’S ALAMO, LP,
                SUSAN CORNWELL AND W. REEGAN BUSBY

                                    TABLE OF CONTENTS

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

                             I. SUMMARY OF CLOSING BRIEF
   Intervenors Naruna Investments, LLC, Scott’s Alamo, LP, Susan Cornwell, and W. Reegan
Busby (collectively, the Naruna Intervenors) limit their participation in this proceeding to opposing
any route that uses Segment U1 (designated Link U1 in the Applicants’ filed route data), namely
Routes 74, 84, 93, 100, 389, 391, 392, 399, 402, 408, 410, 416, 420, 425, 427, 429, 430, 441, 442,
453, 462, 588, 589, and 592. The Naruna Intervenors do not ask the Commission to choose a
uniquely Naruna-preferred route. They ask only that the Administrative Law Judges reject
Segment U1 and recommend a filed route that avoids it.

   The threshold point is dispositive: the Applicants’ own routing engineer identified Route 894
as the route that best meets the statutory criteria, and Commission Staff recommended Route 487.
Both routes avoid Segment U1 entirely. The record contains 98 filed routes that avoid Segment
U1, including the Applicants’ and Staff’s own choices. Eliminating Segment U1 therefore does
not require the Commission to sacrifice length, cost, reliability, or route adequacy.

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                     Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 1 of 11
     Segment U1 is not a close call under the routing factors. It would cut a new diagonal corridor
roughly 1.17 miles across the Naruna ranch, paralleling no existing compatible right-of-way on
the Property, and it appears in 15 of the 20 worst-performing filed routes by paralleling percentage
(75%) despite appearing in only 24 of 122 filed routes (19.7%). It also crosses fixed KWSC public-
water infrastructure that the Applicants did not consult or address, places a habitable structure
within the 500-foot envelope of 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 22.52(a)(3), and burdens
established ranch and recreational uses.

    Nor does any neutral record evidence make Segment U1 necessary. Other landowner-
intervenors oppose it, the U3 proponents reach it only by using U3 as a threshold screen, and the
landowners actually situated on U3 reject every U3 route and urge Route 894. Segment U1 is, in
practical terms, an orphan segment: not selected by the Applicants, not selected by Staff, inferior
on paralleling, and unnecessary to route approval. No party in this record defends Segment U1 on
its merits.

                                  II. ISSUES TO BE ADDRESSED
    In accordance with the Commission’s Order of Referral and Preliminary Order, this brief
addresses the referred issues in the order listed.1

Joint Application
1. Is the joint application adequate, including an adequate number of reasonably differentiated
alternative routes? N/A. The Naruna Intervenors take no position on the adequacy of the
Application.

Notice
2. Did the Applicants provide notice of the joint application in accordance with 16 TAC §
22.52(a)(1), (2), and (3)? N/A.

3. Did the Applicants provide notice of the public meeting in accordance with 16 TAC §
22.52(a)(4)? The Naruna Intervenors’ tracts were not part of the 2025 public-meeting process. The
corridor that crosses them, Segment U1, was added afterward, and the tracts first appeared in the


1
 Because the Naruna Intervenors’ participation is limited, they do not address many of the
referred issues, as indicated below by the “N/A” designation.

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                    Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                 Page 2 of 11
 Application when it was filed on March 26, 2026. The Naruna Intervenors do not contend that
statutory notice of the Application was legally deficient and do not rest their routing case on any
notice question; they note the matter solely to preserve it for the Commission’s consideration
following the Proposal for Decision.

Public Input
4. What were the principal concerns expressed in the questionnaire responses received at or after
the public meetings? N/A.

Need
5. Taking into account the factors in the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA), Tex. Util. Code
§ 37.056(c), are the proposed facilities necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or
safety of the public under PURA § 37.056(a)? N/A.

6. Considering need for a reliability project under PURA § 37.056(c)(2), what are the historical
load, forecasted load growth, and additional load seeking interconnection? N/A.

7. Are the proposed facilities the better option to meet the need when compared to distribution
facilities or a combination of distribution alternatives? N/A.

Route
8. Weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), which
proposed transmission-line route is the best alternative?

   The Commission weighs the statutory routing factors, including community values,
recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, the use of
existing compatible rights-of-way, the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to
consumers, and the prudent avoidance of impacts, and selects the route that best meets them.
(PURA § 37.056(c)(4); 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).) As set out more fully in the direct testimony
of Susan Cornwell (Ex. SC-1 through SC-26), the answer here is narrower than the full route-
selection question: the best alternative is any otherwise adequate filed route that does not use
Segment U1. The Applicants’ and Staff’s own route selections prove that such routes exist.




SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                     Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 3 of 11
    A.    The Applicants’ and Staff’s own route selections prove that Segment U1 is
unnecessary and inferior. The dispositive routing fact is not supplied by Naruna; it is supplied
by the Applicants and Staff. The Applicants’ adopted routing engineer testified that each of the
122 filed routes complies with § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and § 25.101 (Petty Direct at 11-12), and the
Applicants’ panel confirmed at hearing that “all 122 filed routes are acceptable” and satisfy the
legal requirements (Tr. at 108:14-17, 162:10-21 (Perkins) (June 8, 2026)). Applicants identified
Route 894, which does not use Segment U1, as the route that best meets those requirements
(Cornwell Direct §§ V, XIII; Ex. SC-11). At hearing the Applicants’ panel confirmed Route 894
remains “still the panel’s choice.” (Tr. at 94:6-9 (Applicants’ Panel) (June 8, 2026).) Commission
Staff independently preferred a different non-U1 route, Route 487, in part because it “has a
significant amount of parallel right-of-way.” (Tr. at 83:24-84:2 (Poole) (June 10, 2026).)

   That evidence answers the special-treatment objection before it is made. Naruna is not asking
the Commission to invent a new route or impose an outlier accommodation. Ninety-eight filed
routes avoid Segment U1 entirely. (Ex. SC-11.) The Applicants’ own preferred route and Staff’s
recommended route both avoid it. Conversely, every one of the twenty-four routes that carries
Segment U1, including Route 392, would lay this line across the Naruna ranch and should be
eliminated together with the segment. (Petty Direct, Ex. CDP-6, Tbl. 1.) The Commission need
not decide between Route 894 and Route 487 to grant Naruna’s requested relief; it need only
determine that Segment U1 is inferior under the routing criteria and decline to select any route
containing it.

   Naruna does not stand alone. Three other landowner-intervenors affirmatively oppose Segment
U1 on the same routing grounds. Tracy Snell Mack, on behalf of the M.A. Snell Investments Trust
(Intervenor No. 819), appeared in opposition to Segment U1. (Tr. at 18:22-24 (June 9, 2026); Tracy
Snell Mack Ex. 1.) Crawford Partners, LP and SF Eastside Investments, LLC have each filed in
opposition to Segment U1, on the grounds that the segment fails to parallel existing compatible
corridors and was added late to the routing process. (Crawford Partners Statement of Position; SF
Eastside Investments Statement of Position.) Dance Bar Ranch, LLC asks the Commission to deny
the Application or, in the alternative, to reject any route that uses Link V1 - a segment carried only
by Routes 392, 402, 410, and 416, each of which also carries Segment U1. (Dance Bar Ranch
Initial Br. at 1, 8; Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1 at 2780-2781.) The landowners situated on Link U3

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                      Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                   Page 4 of 11
 likewise reject every U3 route, which necessarily traverses Segment U1, and urge approval of
Route 894, and the Theon-Voss and D & M Davis Land and Cattle interests also support Route
894. (Rowntree Direct at 7 (U3L-1); Tr. at 275:18-21 (June 11, 2026).) No party in this record
defends Segment U1 on its merits.

   The Applicants’ own Environmental Assessment confirms the point. Segment U1 was not part
of the preliminary routing but was added after the public meetings for “additional routing
diversity” - not necessity. (Cornwell Direct § V; Tr. at 184:8-185:2 (Applicants’ Panel) (June 9,
2026).) The Commission’s authority is not limited to choosing among the filed routes; it may deny
a transmission-line application in its entirety, as it did to this same applicant in the Gillespie-
Newton CREZ case. See Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corp., PUC Docket No.
37448, Final Order at Conclusion of Law No. 8A (Apr. 26, 2010) (Ex. CRAI-9, CRAI-11, CRAI-
12; BCI-62). If the Commission may reject an entire filing, it may far more readily decline to select
any route built on a single, admittedly unnecessary segment that the Applicants’ own preferred
route already avoids.

   B. The request to cross the Colorado River at Link U3 must be rejected, because the
screen used to justify it discards Route 894 and forces Segment U1 across the Naruna ranch.
Solana Ranch and the Brady Creek Intervenors (Wulff Bluff Creek Ranch and Abell Ranches) ask
the Commission to reject Route 894 and to cross the Colorado River at Link U3 instead, on the
ground that U3 is the least-harm crossing. (Rhodes Direct at 14 (Solana Ex. 4); Sansom Direct at
18-20 (Brady Creek Ex. 3).) The argument rests on a single screening premise that the proponents’
own routing engineer dismantled on cross-examination. Joshua Rhodes testified that he made
“utilizing Link U3” his step-one screen - the “differentiating factor” he applied before any
paralleling or property-line analysis. This one screen, by itself, removes Route 894 and every other
filed route except the twelve that use Link U3. (Tr. at 73:20-74:9, 81:23-82:8 (Rhodes) (June 11,
2026).) He further conceded that, had the Commission instead weighed all 122 routes on the
statutory factors, his analysis would not have eliminated Route 894; that screening on U3 was his
own “personal preference”; and that he never placed Route 392 and Route 894 side by side. (Tr.
at 74:1-21 (Rhodes) (June 11, 2026).) The case for Route 392 thus depends entirely on accepting
U3 as a threshold filter instead of weighing the routes the way the statute requires.



SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                     Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 5 of 11
    That filter is flawed for two reasons. First, it is a Segment U1 filter in disguise: every one of
the twelve routes that survives the U3 screen carries Segment U1 across the Naruna ranch,
including Route 392 itself, which the proponents’ own engineer concedes is built on Link U3.
(Turnbough Direct at 13 (Brady Creek Ex. 4); Petty Direct, Ex. CDP-6, Tbl. 1.) Second, even the
narrow crossing claim does not hold up. The proponents’ conservation witness, Andrew Sansom,
limited his “least harm” opinion to the single crossing link and offered no opinion on the best
overall route (Sansom Direct at 18-20 (Brady Creek Ex. 3)). Additionally, on the proponents’ own
figures, Route 392 is longer than Route 894 (229.02 versus 223.17 miles) and carries 136 habitable
structures within 500 feet against 85 for Route 894 - some 60% more (Turnbough Direct at 14
(Brady Creek Ex. 4)). The landowners actually situated on Link U3 reject every U3 route and ask
the Commission to approve Route 894, because all twelve U3 routes cost more and affect more
habitable structures than Route 894. (Rowntree Direct at 7, 22 (U3L-1).) The Commission should
reject Link U3, reject Segment U1, and select a non-U1 route.

   C. Segment U1 parallels no existing compatible right-of-way and is among the worst
paralleling performers in the filing. Section 25.101(b)(3)(B) expresses a preference, where
reasonable, for the use of existing compatible rights-of-way, a category the rule expressly includes
railroad rights-of-way. Across Segment U1’s full 17.87-mile length, the Applicants’ own
Appendix E, Table 7-3 reports zero feet of paralleling to any railroad and zero feet to any pipeline.
Across the Naruna ranch, Segment U1 parallels nothing at all. (Cornwell Direct § V; Ex. SC-2.)
The available corridors - the existing Oncor 345-kV Brown-Killeen line (owned by an Applicant),
the Matterhorn and Seminole pipelines, and the BNSF Lampasas Subdivision - were drawn near
but not used. (Cornwell Direct § V.)

   The Applicants’ own route data shows the consequence: although Segment U1 is in only 24 of
the 122 filed routes (19.7%), it appears in 15 of the 20 worst-performing routes ranked by
paralleling percentage (75%). (Ex. SC-25; Petty Direct, Ex. CDP-6 (Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 5),
Tbls. 1-2.) The Applicants’ adopted routing memorandum confirms the pattern at the corridor
level: the northern Link U6 corridor - whose routes carry Segment U1 - parallels existing
compatible right-of-way for only 29.1% to 44.6% of route length, the lowest band of the five filed
corridors. (Petty Direct, Ex. CDP-6 at 42, adopted by witness Perkins at the June 8, 2026 hearing.)
Not one of the 122 filed routes parallels a railroad for any distance at all. (Petty Direct, Ex. CDP-

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                     Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 6 of 11
 6, Tbl. 2.) The Staff-selected non-U1 Route 487 prioritized the very factor on which Segment U1
performs worst.

   D. Segment U1 would place a 765-kV line on fixed KWSC public-water infrastructure
that the Applicants did not identify or evaluate. On the Naruna Property, KWSC holds recorded
fee title (1.38 acres), a recorded access easement (0.78 acre), and perpetual right-of-way easements
over 1,110 acres, each granted on USDA-Farmers Home Administration forms reciting federal
financial assistance. (Cornwell Direct §§ VII, XII; Ex. SC-12, SC-13, SC-14.) KWSC’s water
system on the Property - the two Hewgley tanks, an active pump station, and metered mains - is
the fourth-largest production point on a system serving roughly 25,000 residents across four
counties. (Ex. SC-5, SC-17, SC-18.)

   The routing consequence is concrete. A 765-kV transmission line across Segment U1 would
require tower foundations, construction access, laydown areas, vegetation clearing, and long-term
maintenance in the same fixed area as KWSC’s water-production facilities and recorded
easements. (Cornwell Direct § VII.) Those surveyed KWSC interests cannot be moved by a minor
centerline adjustment, and a route that avoids Segment U1 avoids the conflict entirely. (Cornwell
Direct § VII.) Although PURA § 37.056(c) and the Commission’s rules require routing to account
for environmental integrity, including water resources, the Applicants’ Environmental Assessment
is silent on the KWSC public-water system that provides drinking water to thousands of customers.
Appendix A to the Application reflects outreach to dozens of agencies, but the Applicants never
consulted KWSC or the Naruna Intervenors about this infrastructure. (Cornwell Direct §§ VII,
XII.) The Applicants’ panel admitted that a planned use of which they were unaware “was not
considered,” and that “if a land use is not considered, it cannot be avoided through routing.” (Tr.
at 28:21-29:14 (Applicants’ Panel) (June 8, 2026).)

   Segment U1 also places a habitable structure - Trailer-Mounted Hunting Cabin No. 2, at
approximately 369 feet (Ex. SC-3A; Ex. SC-7) - within the 500-foot envelope that 16 TAC §
22.52(a)(3) treats as the zone of direct effect, and would site the line approximately 266 feet from
a planned residence (Ex. SC-7; Ex. SC-16), neither of which the Applicants inventoried (Cornwell
Direct §§ VI, IX, XII). It also burdens community values documented by State Senator Pete
Flores’s letter, three county resolutions, and the community’s reliance on KWSC water (Ex. SC-


SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                    Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                 Page 7 of 11
 24; Cornwell Direct § VIII); disrupts an established commercial deer- and waterfowl-hunting
operation supported by twenty-seven pieces of fixed infrastructure, including a heavily used duck-
hunting stock tank approximately 310 feet from the line (Ex. SC-6, SC-7, SC-8, SC-26; Cornwell
Direct § IX); fragments mature oak stands managed under a USDA-NRCS conservation plan and
prescribed-burn program (Ex. SC-9, SC-21, SC-22; Cornwell Direct § X); and impairs the
historical character and high-point viewshed of a century-old family ranch (Ex. SC-10; Cornwell
Direct § XI). Because 765-kV transmission is unprecedented in Texas - the Applicants conceded
“no real-life experience” with its effects (Tr. at 84:8-15 (Applicants’ Panel) (June 8, 2026)) - this
proximity to homes, water, and waterfowl weighs against Segment U1, not for it. These
considerations reinforce, but are not essential to, the core routing problem: the Commission has
superior non-U1 choices already in the record.



9. Are there alternative routes or configurations that would have a less negative effect on
landowners? What would be the incremental cost of those routes?

   Yes. The evidentiary record supports a choice of non-U1 alternatives with fewer habitable
structures, shorter length, lower cost, and more paralleling. On the Applicants’ own corridor data,
each of the four non-U6 corridors begins at both a shorter minimum length and a lower minimum
estimated cost than the lowest Link U6 (U1) route. (Petty Direct, Ex. CDP-6 at 41-42.) Routes 894
and 487 therefore achieve a less negative effect on landowners at no incremental length or cost.
Avoiding Segment U1 carries no penalty to the Project.

10. If alternative routes are considered because of individual landowners’ preferences, have those
landowners made adequate contributions to offset additional costs, and have the accommodations
diminished electrical efficiency or reliability? N/A.



Cost to Consumers

11. Are the proposed facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards? N/A.

12. What is the estimated cost of the proposed facilities to consumers? N/A.

13. What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers? N/A.

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                     Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                  Page 8 of 11
 Best Management Practices
14. Are the standard best management practices for construction and operation adequate, and if
not, what additional practices should be required? N/A.

15. For each additional practice proposed, what is its added cost, benefit, and effect on reliability,
design, construction, and the energization date? N/A.



Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
16. Did the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department provide recommendations or informational
comments under section 12.0011(b) of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Code? N/A.



Permits
17. What permits, licenses, plans, or permission will be required for construction and operation,
and what is the status of any required state or federal agency permission? N/A.



Coastal Management Program
18. Is any part of the proposed facilities located within the coastal management program boundary
as defined in 31 TAC § 27.1(a)? N/A.



Limitation of Authority
19. Are the circumstances such that the seven-year limit discussed in the Order should be changed?
N/A.



Other Issues
20. Will anything occur during construction that will preclude or limit a generator from generating
or delivering power, or that will adversely affect the reliability of the ERCOT system? N/A.

21. If agreement is reached on a route relying on modifications to noticed route segments, were
the additional notice and written-consent requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) satisfied? N/A.


SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                      Naruna Intervenors’ Closing Brief
PUC Docket No. 59475                                                                   Page 9 of 11
                                         III. CONCLUSION
    The Naruna Intervenors recognize the importance of reliable transmission infrastructure. But
this case does not require a tradeoff between transmission need and route adequacy. The
Applicants and Staff have already identified filed routes that satisfy the statutory criteria and avoid
Segment U1. The Commission need not decide between Route 894 and Route 487 to grant
Naruna’s requested relief; it need only determine that Segment U1 is inferior under the routing
criteria and decline to select any route containing it.

    Accordingly, the Naruna Intervenors respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges
issue a Proposal for Decision (1) rejecting Segment U1 and every route containing Segment U1,
including Route 392; (2) recommending Route 894, Route 487, or another filed route that avoids
Segment U1; and (3) granting such other and further relief to which the Naruna Intervenors may
be entitled.

recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, the use of
existing compatible rights-of-way, the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to
consumers, and the prudent avoidance of impacts, and selects the route that best meets them.
(PURA § 37.056(c)(4); 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).) As set out more fully in the direct testimony
of Susan Cornwell (Ex. SC-1 through SC-26), the answer here is narrower than the full route-
selection question: the best alternative is any otherwise adequate filed route that does not use
Segment Ul. The Applicants' and Staff' s own route selections prove that such routes exist.

                                         III. CONCLUSION

    The Naruna Intervenors recognize the importance of reliable transmission infrastructure. But
this case does not require a tradeoff between transmission need and route adequacy. The
Applicants and Staffhave already identified filed routes that satisfy the statutory criteria and avoid
Segment Ul. The Commission need not decide between Route 894 and Route 487 to grant
Naruna' s requested relief; it need only determine that Segment Ul is inferior under the routing
criteria and decline to select any route containing it.

    Accordingly, the Naruna Intervenors respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges
issue a Proposal for Decision (1) rejecting Segment Ul and every route containing Segment Ul,
including Route 392; (2) recommending Route 894, Route 487, or another filed route that avoids
Segment Ul; and (3) granting such other and further relief to which the Naruna Intervenors may
be entitled.
